children.text: RF reflectometry for spin readout for silicon quantum computing

Model lossless TEM transmission lines and ideal circuit elements. A coaxial line has inner-core radius a and shield inner radius b, filled with relative permittivity εr and permeability μr. Ignore conductor resistance, internal inductance and dielectric leakage. Use ε=ε0εr, μ=μ0μr, c0=1/√(ε0μ0), with ε0=\(8.854\times10^{-12}\) F/m and μ0=\(4\pi\times10^{-7}\) H/m. Reflection coefficients are voltage-amplitude ratios, including phase, not power ratios. For phasors use exp(iωt), so a capacitor has impedance 1/(iωC). The SET and SLQD circuit diagrams specify which elements are in series and parallel. Use \(\epsilon=\epsilon_0\epsilon_r\), \(\mu=\mu_0\mu_r\), and \(\Gamma=V_r/V_i\).
Find the electromagnetic propagation speed in the cable.
A length Δx of core carries charge Δq and the outer shield is grounded. Find E(r) between the conductors.

statement.text:
RF reflectometry for spin readout for silicon quantum computing
Model lossless TEM transmission lines and ideal circuit elements. A coaxial line has inner-core radius a and shield inner radius b, filled with relative permittivity εr and permeability μr. Ignore conductor resistance, internal inductance and dielectric leakage. Use ε=ε0εr, μ=μ0μr, c0=1/√(ε0μ0), with ε0=\(8.854\times10^{-12}\) F/m and μ0=\(4\pi\times10^{-7}\) H/m. Reflection coefficients are voltage-amplitude ratios, including phase, not power ratios. For phasors use exp(iωt), so a capacitor has impedance 1/(iωC). The SET and SLQD circuit diagrams specify which elements are in series and parallel. Use \(\epsilon=\epsilon_0\epsilon_r\), \(\mu=\mu_0\mu_r\), and \(\Gamma=V_r/V_i\).
a.1. Wave speed
Find the electromagnetic propagation speed in the cable.
a.2. Coaxial electric field
A length Δx of core carries charge Δq and the outer shield is grounded. Find E(r) between the conductors.
a.3. Capacitance per length
Find Cx.
a.4. Inductance per length
Find Lx.
a.5. Characteristic impedance

Use the short-section ladder to show Z0=√(Lx/Cx). For Z0=50 Ω, εr=4, μr=1 calculate b/a.
b.1. Wire above ground plane

A thin wire of radius a lies distance d≫a from an infinite grounded plane in the same medium. Find its characteristic impedance.
c.1. Voltage reflection coefficient
A line of real impedance Z0 joins a line of impedance Z1. Derive Γ=Vr/Vi.
c.2. Reflection phase inversion
For positive real impedances, when does reflection introduce a π phase shift?
d.1. Quantum-dot potential and addition energy

A quantum dot has n excess electrons, total capacitance Cg dominated by its gate at voltage Vg. Source and drain are grounded and tunnel capacitances Ct≪Cg. Find φn and the energy to add one electron.
d.2. Equilibrium addition-energy scale
Electrons enter until the smallest integer N with ΔEN≥0 is reached. Find the maximum achievable equilibrium addition-energy scale Ec as Vg varies.
d.3. Thermal condition
Give the temperature condition for a strong distinction between ON and OFF states.
d.4. Tunnelling time and resistance
Estimate the tunnel-junction time from Rt,Ct. Using the source's lifetime broadening h/τ, find the resistance condition to preserve distinct addition energies.
e.1. Bare SET reflection contrast
The SET is Ron=100 kΩ when ON and open-circuit when OFF, connected directly to Z0=50 Ω. Find ΔΓ=|Γon−Γoff|.
e.2. Series-inductor matching circuit

Add series L0 before the parallel combination of C0=0.4 pF and the SET. At f=100 MHz estimate L0 for order-one ΔΓ, and compute the resulting contrast.
f.1. Single-lead quantum-dot readout

In the SLQD circuit L0,C0 and the dot are all in parallel. The dot is open when OFF and a capacitance Cq when ON. With C0 fixed, suggest ωrf and ZC=√(L0/C0) for ΔΓ of order one.
f.2. Additional matching element
If the fixed inductance gives ZC much smaller than Z0Cq/C0, draw where to add one element and specify its value to retain ΔΓ of order one.

children.text: RF reflectometry for spin readout for silicon quantum computing
Gauss's law on a cylindrical surface gives \(E(r)=\Delta q/(2\pi\epsilon\Delta x\,r)\), radially outward for positive charge.
The core potential is \(\Delta q\ln(b/a)/(2\pi\epsilon\Delta x)\). Hence \(C_x=2\pi\epsilon/\ln(b/a)\).
Between the conductors \(B(r)=\mu I/(2\pi r)\). Integrating flux per unit length gives \(L_x=\mu\ln(b/a)/(2\pi)\).

Appending a short cell with series iωLx dx and shunt iωCx dx must leave the semi-infinite impedance unchanged. To first order this gives Lx−CxZ0²=0. Thus \(Z_0=\ln(b/a)\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}/(2\pi)\). Since √(μ0/ε0)/(2π)=59.96 Ω, \(b/a=\exp[50\sqrt4/59.96]\simeq5.30\).

Replace the plane by opposite charge and opposite return current in an image wire 2d away. To leading order \(C_x=2\pi\epsilon/\ln(2d/a)\), \(L_x=\mu\ln(2d/a)/(2\pi)\). Therefore \[Z_0=\frac{\ln(2d/a)}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac\mu\epsilon}.\]
Voltage continuity gives Vi+Vr=Vt, current continuity gives (Vi−Vr)/Z0=Vt/Z1. Thus \(\Gamma=(Z_1-Z_0)/(Z_1+Z_0)\). The reflected current has the opposite propagation direction.
A π shift means Γ<0, occurring for Z1<Z0. At Z1=Z0 reflection vanishes, so a reflected phase is not defined.
d.1. Quantum-dot potential and addition energy

With electron charge −e, \(\phi_n=V_g-ne/C_g\). Integrate the potential while adding charge −e, or average the initial and final potentials: \[\Delta E_n=-e(\phi_n+\phi_{n+1})/2=\frac{e^2}{C_g}(n+1/2)-eV_g.\] The voltage source's work must be included.

Addition energies are spaced by e²/Cg. As a gate threshold is crossed, N increments and ΔEN resets from approximately zero to approximately e²/Cg. Thus \(E_c=e^2/C_g\), understood as the supremum of this sawtooth if exact degeneracy is assigned to the lower-N state.
Thermal excitations must be much smaller than the addition energy: \(k_BT\ll E_c=e^2/C_g\). Near a particular gate degeneracy the actual ΔEN, rather than its maximum, sets the stricter condition.

\(\tau\sim R_tC_t\). Requiring \(h/(R_tC_t)\ll e^2/C_g\) gives \(R_t\gg hC_g/(e^2C_t)\), which is stronger than h/e² because Cg≫Ct. This uses the specifically requested junction-capacitance time estimate.

Tune the OFF series LC resonance: \(L_0=1/(\omega^2C_0)=6.33\,\mu H\), giving Zoff=0 and Γoff=−1. In the ON state \(Z_{on}=i\omega L_0+[1/R_{on}+i\omega C_0]^{-1}\simeq(158+6.3i)\,\Omega\). Thus Γon≈0.520+0.0145i and ΔΓ≈1.52. The contrast can exceed one because it is a difference of complex amplitudes.

Tune \(\omega_{rf}=1/\sqrt{L_0C_0}\), so the OFF admittance vanishes and Γoff=1. ON impedance is \(Z_{on}=1/(i\omega_{rf}C_q)=-iZ_CC_0/C_q\). Make its magnitude comparable to Z0: \(Z_C\sim Z_0C_q/C_0\). At equality Γon=−i and ΔΓ=√2 in the stated phasor convention.

Add a capacitor Cm in series between the transmission line and the entire parallel LC-dot network. At the same OFF resonance the network remains open, so Γoff=1. ON impedance is \(-i[1/(\omega C_q)+1/(\omega C_m)]\). Set its magnitude to Z0: \[C_m=\frac{C_q}{Z_0\omega C_q-1}\simeq\frac1{Z_0\omega}.\] The assumed inequality ensures Cm>0. Then Γon=−i and ΔΓ=√2. The source's +i uses the opposite phasor sign and does not change the contrast.

solution.text:
RF reflectometry for spin readout for silicon quantum computing
a.1. Wave speed
TEM propagation speed is \(v=1/\sqrt{\epsilon\mu}=c_0/\sqrt{\epsilon_r\mu_r}\).
a.2. Coaxial electric field
Gauss's law on a cylindrical surface gives \(E(r)=\Delta q/(2\pi\epsilon\Delta x\,r)\), radially outward for positive charge.
a.3. Capacitance per length
The core potential is \(\Delta q\ln(b/a)/(2\pi\epsilon\Delta x)\). Hence \(C_x=2\pi\epsilon/\ln(b/a)\).
a.4. Inductance per length
Between the conductors \(B(r)=\mu I/(2\pi r)\). Integrating flux per unit length gives \(L_x=\mu\ln(b/a)/(2\pi)\).
a.5. Characteristic impedance
Appending a short cell with series iωLx dx and shunt iωCx dx must leave the semi-infinite impedance unchanged. To first order this gives Lx−CxZ0²=0. Thus \(Z_0=\ln(b/a)\sqrt{\mu/\epsilon}/(2\pi)\). Since √(μ0/ε0)/(2π)=59.96 Ω, \(b/a=\exp[50\sqrt4/59.96]\simeq5.30\).
b.1. Wire above ground plane
Replace the plane by opposite charge and opposite return current in an image wire 2d away. To leading order \(C_x=2\pi\epsilon/\ln(2d/a)\), \(L_x=\mu\ln(2d/a)/(2\pi)\). Therefore \[Z_0=\frac{\ln(2d/a)}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac\mu\epsilon}.\]
c.1. Voltage reflection coefficient
Voltage continuity gives Vi+Vr=Vt, current continuity gives (Vi−Vr)/Z0=Vt/Z1. Thus \(\Gamma=(Z_1-Z_0)/(Z_1+Z_0)\). The reflected current has the opposite propagation direction.
c.2. Reflection phase inversion
A π shift means Γ<0, occurring for Z1<Z0. At Z1=Z0 reflection vanishes, so a reflected phase is not defined.
d.1. Quantum-dot potential and addition energy
With electron charge −e, \(\phi_n=V_g-ne/C_g\). Integrate the potential while adding charge −e, or average the initial and final potentials: \[\Delta E_n=-e(\phi_n+\phi_{n+1})/2=\frac{e^2}{C_g}(n+1/2)-eV_g.\] The voltage source's work must be included.
d.2. Equilibrium addition-energy scale
Addition energies are spaced by e²/Cg. As a gate threshold is crossed, N increments and ΔEN resets from approximately zero to approximately e²/Cg. Thus \(E_c=e^2/C_g\), understood as the supremum of this sawtooth if exact degeneracy is assigned to the lower-N state.
d.3. Thermal condition
Thermal excitations must be much smaller than the addition energy: \(k_BT\ll E_c=e^2/C_g\). Near a particular gate degeneracy the actual ΔEN, rather than its maximum, sets the stricter condition.
d.4. Tunnelling time and resistance
\(\tau\sim R_tC_t\). Requiring \(h/(R_tC_t)\ll e^2/C_g\) gives \(R_t\gg hC_g/(e^2C_t)\), which is stronger than h/e² because Cg≫Ct. This uses the specifically requested junction-capacitance time estimate.
e.1. Bare SET reflection contrast
Γoff=1 and Γon=(100000−50)/(100000+50). Thus \(\Delta\Gamma=100/100050\simeq9.995\times10^{-4}\).
e.2. Series-inductor matching circuit
Tune the OFF series LC resonance: \(L_0=1/(\omega^2C_0)=6.33\,\mu H\), giving Zoff=0 and Γoff=−1. In the ON state \(Z_{on}=i\omega L_0+[1/R_{on}+i\omega C_0]^{-1}\simeq(158+6.3i)\,\Omega\). Thus Γon≈0.520+0.0145i and ΔΓ≈1.52. The contrast can exceed one because it is a difference of complex amplitudes.
f.1. Single-lead quantum-dot readout
Tune \(\omega_{rf}=1/\sqrt{L_0C_0}\), so the OFF admittance vanishes and Γoff=1. ON impedance is \(Z_{on}=1/(i\omega_{rf}C_q)=-iZ_CC_0/C_q\). Make its magnitude comparable to Z0: \(Z_C\sim Z_0C_q/C_0\). At equality Γon=−i and ΔΓ=√2 in the stated phasor convention.
f.2. Additional matching element
Add a capacitor Cm in series between the transmission line and the entire parallel LC-dot network. At the same OFF resonance the network remains open, so Γoff=1. ON impedance is \(-i[1/(\omega C_q)+1/(\omega C_m)]\). Set its magnitude to Z0: \[C_m=\frac{C_q}{Z_0\omega C_q-1}\simeq\frac1{Z_0\omega}.\] The assumed inequality ensures Cm>0. Then Γon=−i and ΔΓ=√2. The source's +i uses the opposite phasor sign and does not change the contrast.
